newsitem.title: UK: Major talks tough before decision on working week.
newsitem.headline: Major talks tough before decision on working week.

text.p: Britons used to working shifts of 10 or more hours on Monday awaited a key European Court ruling on whether working hours should be limited -- none of them more keenly than Prime Minister John Major.
A court judgment that the average working week should be no longer than 48 hours would ease the burden on 3.8 million Britons who work longer than that.
But it would also reignite the row over Europe's encroachment on British sovereignty which has repeatedly threatened to split Major's Conservative Party.
And Major could find himself in a battle with the Union which could prove crucial to his hopes of winning a general election he must call within the next six months.

The Luxembourg-based court is widely expected to rule that European Union regulations setting a 48-hour week and laying down minimum holiday and break periods were correctly adopted and that Britain, like it or not, must abide by them.
Major claims as one of his big achievements the negotiation of a right for Britain to opt out of EU working practices legislation enshrined in its so-called Social Chapter.
But the maximum work week provisions were brought in under health and safety provisions of the EU's founding treaty to which Britain is, like other EU countries, subject.
Britain has told the court that the issue has nothing to do with health and safety, and was therefore wrongly adopted.

"I am determined not just to maintain our Social Chapter opt-out but to stand firm against the use of other treaty articles to impose employment regulations by the back door," Major wrote in an article in the Daily Telegraph on Monday.
Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine told BBC radio that if Tuesday's ruling went against the government, it would attempt to get it reversed at the inter-governmental conference.

Asked whether this meant Britain would disrupt the IGC to get its way, he said: "It is not a question of disruption. We are in Europe for Britain's self interest and when we get to the IGC we will fight for Britain's corner."

The Telegraph, a Conservative-supporting newspaper which takes a generally Eurosceptic stance, suggested on Monday that Major should go further, repealing a provision of a 1972 act of parliament enshrining the supremacy of EU law in Britain.
"As long as the 1972 Act remains unamended, the sovereignty of Britain lies with an unelected group of judges who can change the law as they please," it said in an editorial.

Opposition politicians accuse the government of exaggerating the impact the rules would have, pointing out that workers who agree to work longer hours without pressure from employers may do so, and that there are exemptions for certain industries.

"It is the right of an individual not to have to work for more than 48 hours in certain circumstances where there are not exemptions," Gordon Brown, economics spokesman for the opposition Labour Party, said.
But Britain's largest trade union, Unison, said this week it was preparing to take the government to court in Britain if it failed to implement the rules when they come into force on November 23.
